choices.text: In the elimination of HX from an alkyl halide, the more highly substituted alkene product predominates
In the elimination of HX from an alkyl halide, the less highly substituted alkene product predominates
choices.why: That's the reverse. Base-induced eliminations generally give the more stable, more substituted alkene.

choices.text: In the addition of HX to an alkene, the H adds to the carbon that has more hydrogens
choices.why: That is Markovnikov's rule, which is about additions, not eliminations.

choices.text: In the elimination of HX from an alkyl halide, a single alkene forms with no other products
choices.why: Eliminations almost always give mixtures of alkenes. Zaitsev's rule predicts which one is major.

explanation: According to Zaitsev's rule (1875), base-induced elimination reactions generally, although not always, give the more stable alkene product, the one with more alkyl substituents on the double-bond carbons.

prompt: When 2-bromobutane is treated with sodium ethoxide in ethanol, what percent of the alkene product is 2-butene?
explanation: 2-Bromobutane gives 2-butene (81%) and 1-butene (19%). The disubstituted 2-butene, the more highly substituted alkene, predominates, as Zaitsev's rule predicts.

prompt: Which alkene is the major product when 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH3)2CBrCH2CH3, is treated with sodium ethoxide in ethanol?

choices.why: That disubstituted alkene is the minor product. The trisubstituted 2-methyl-2-butene predominates.
The double bond must include carbon 2, which held the bromine. 3-Methyl-1-butene's double bond doesn't.
That would be a substitution product. The section's example with ethoxide gives a mixture of two alkenes.

explanation: Loss of HBr gives 2-methyl-2-butene (70%), with three alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons, and 2-methyl-1-butene (30%), with two. The more highly substituted alkene predominates.

prompt: When 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is treated with sodium ethoxide in ethanol, what percent of the alkene product is 2-methyl-1-butene?
explanation: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane gives 2-methyl-2-butene (70%) and 2-methyl-1-butene (30%). The less substituted 2-methyl-1-butene is the minor product.

prompt: In the E1 reaction, in what order are the C–H and C–X bonds broken?

choices.text: The C–X bond breaks first to give a carbocation, then a base removes H+
Both bonds break at the same time, in a single step
choices.why: That is the E2 reaction.

choices.text: The C–H bond breaks first to give a carbanion, then X− leaves
choices.why: That is the E1cB reaction.

choices.text: The C–H bond breaks first to give a carbocation, then X− leaves
choices.why: Removing H+ leaves an electron pair behind, giving a carbanion, not a carbocation. In E1 the C–X bond breaks first.

explanation: The E1, E2 and E1cB mechanisms differ in the timing of C–H and C–X bond breaking. In the E1 reaction, the C–X bond breaks first to give a carbocation intermediate, which then undergoes base abstraction of H+ to yield the alkene.

prompt: In the E2 reaction, how are the C–H and C–X bonds broken?

choices.text: At the same time, giving the alkene in a single step
The C–X bond first, giving a carbocation, then the C–H bond
choices.why: That is the E1 reaction.

choices.text: The C–H bond first, giving a carbanion, then the C–X bond
choices.why: That is the E1cB reaction.

choices.text: Only the C–H bond; the C–X bond stays intact in the alkene
choices.why: Elimination of HX means the halogen leaves too.

explanation: In the E2 reaction, base-induced C–H bond cleavage is simultaneous with C–X bond cleavage, giving the alkene in a single step.

prompt: What does "cB" stand for in E1cB, and what intermediate forms?

choices.text: Conjugate base; a carbanion forms when the proton is removed first
Conjugate base; a carbocation forms when X− leaves first
choices.why: In E1cB the proton is removed first, giving a carbanion. A carbocation forms in E1.

choices.text: Carbocation, bimolecular; a carbocation forms when X− leaves first
choices.why: cB stands for conjugate base, and the intermediate is a carbanion.
cB stands for conjugate base. The reaction does have an intermediate, a carbanion.

explanation: In the E1cB reaction (cB for "conjugate base"), base abstraction of the proton occurs first, giving a carbanion (R:−) intermediate. This anion, the conjugate base of the reactant "acid," then loses X− to give the alkene.

prompt: Which elimination mechanism predominates in biological pathways?

choices.why: E1 reactions occur frequently in the laboratory, but E1cB predominates in biological pathways.
E2 reactions occur frequently in the laboratory, but E1cB predominates in biological pathways.
All three occur frequently in the laboratory, but in biological pathways E1cB predominates.

explanation: All three mechanisms, E1, E2 and E1cB, occur frequently in the laboratory, but the E1cB mechanism predominates in biological pathways.

prompt: What is the major product when 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane reacts with KOH in ethanol?

choices.why: That is the minor product. Its double bond carries only two alkyl substituents, versus three in 1-methylcyclohexene.
The double bond must include carbon 1, which held the chlorine. 3-Methylcyclohexene's double bond doesn't.
That would be a substitution product. Treating the alkyl halide with the strong base KOH gives alkenes here.

explanation: Locate the hydrogens on each carbon next to the leaving group and remove HX in each possible way. Removing H from a ring carbon gives 1-methylcyclohexene (trisubstituted, major); removing H from the methyl gives methylenecyclohexane (disubstituted, minor) (Worked Example 11.7.1).

prompt: Ignoring double-bond stereochemistry, what is the major elimination product of 3-bromo-2-methylpentane, (CH3)2CHCHBrCH2CH3?

choices.why: That disubstituted alkene is the minor product. Removing the H from carbon 2 gives the trisubstituted 2-methyl-2-pentene.
The double bond must include carbon 3, which held the bromine. A double bond between carbons 1 and 2 doesn't.
Elimination doesn't change the carbon skeleton, so the product must be a methylpentene.

explanation: The β carbons are carbon 2 (one H) and carbon 4 (two H's). Loss of H from carbon 2 gives 2-methyl-2-pentene, with three alkyl groups on the double bond (major); loss from carbon 4 gives 4-methyl-2-pentene, with two (minor) (Exercise 11.7.1).

prompt: What is the major elimination product of 3-chloro-2,3,5-trimethylhexane, (CH3)2CHCCl(CH3)CH2CH(CH3)2?

choices.why: That trisubstituted alkene is a minor product. The tetrasubstituted 2,3,5-trimethyl-2-hexene predominates.
That disubstituted alkene, from loss of a methyl hydrogen, is a minor product.
The double bond must include carbon 3, which held the chlorine. Carbon 1 isn't next to carbon 3.

explanation: Removing H from carbon 2 gives 2,3,5-trimethyl-2-hexene, with four alkyl groups on the double bond (major). Removing H from carbon 4 gives 2,3,5-trimethyl-3-hexene (three), and from the 3-methyl group gives 2-isopropyl-4-methyl-1-pentene (two) (Exercise 11.7.1).

prompt: Ignoring double-bond stereochemistry, how many different alkenes can form by elimination of HCl from 3-chloro-2,3,5-trimethylhexane, (CH3)2CHCCl(CH3)CH2CH(CH3)2?
explanation: The chlorine-bearing carbon 3 has three different neighboring carbons with hydrogens: carbon 2, carbon 4 and the 3-methyl group. They give 2,3,5-trimethyl-2-hexene (major), 2,3,5-trimethyl-3-hexene and 2-isopropyl-4-methyl-1-pentene.

prompt: What is the major elimination product of (1-bromoethyl)cyclohexane, C6H11CH(Br)CH3, where C6H11 is a cyclohexyl ring?

choices.why: That monosubstituted alkene, from loss of a CH3 hydrogen, is the minor product.
The double bond must include the side-chain carbon that held the bromine. 1-Ethylcyclohexene's double bond lies entirely in the ring.
That is a substitution product, not an elimination product.

explanation: Removing the H from the ring carbon gives ethylidenecyclohexane, with three alkyl groups on the double bond (major). Removing an H from the CH3 gives cyclohexylethylene, C6H11CH=CH2, with only one (minor) (Exercise 11.7.1).

prompt: Which alkyl halide would give only 3,6-dimethyl-1-heptene, CH2=CHCH(CH3)CH2CH2CH(CH3)2, on elimination of HBr?

choices.why: Elimination could then also form a carbon 2–carbon 3 double bond, and Zaitsev's rule says that more substituted alkene would predominate.
Carbon 1 isn't next to carbon 3, so no double bond between carbons 1 and 2 could form.
That would give 2,5-dimethyl-1-heptene; the methyl groups would be on the wrong carbons.

explanation: With Br on carbon 1, the only neighboring carbon with hydrogens is carbon 2, so elimination can only give the 1-alkene, 3,6-dimethyl-1-heptene (Exercise 11.7.2).

prompt: Applying Zaitsev's rule, what is the major alkene from base-induced elimination of HBr from 2-bromo-2-methylpentane, (CH3)2CBrCH2CH2CH3?

choices.why: That alkene has only two alkyl groups on its double bond. 2-Methyl-2-pentene, with three, predominates.
The double bond must include carbon 2, which held the bromine. 4-Methyl-2-pentene's double bond doesn't.
Elimination doesn't move the methyl group; the product keeps the 2-methylpentane skeleton.

explanation: Loss of H from carbon 3 gives (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH3, 2-methyl-2-pentene, with three alkyl substituents on the double bond. Loss of H from a methyl group gives 2-methyl-1-pentene, with two. By Zaitsev's rule the more highly substituted 2-methyl-2-pentene predominates.
